title: Measuring Verifier Impact in an LLM Generate→Verify→Repair Loop for Intent→Configuration NetOps Tasks
abstract: We measure the marginal effect of inserting a deterministic network verifier (plus at most one automated repair iteration) into a generate→verify→repair (G→V→R) loop for LLM-produced device-configuration proposals. Using a preregistered paired design on a deterministic synthetic corpus (N = 500 intent→configuration tasks stratified into VLAN-change, ACL-change, and static-route-change clusters) and shared_initial_candidate semantics, we compared: (1) baseline — the single LLM proposal treated as the final output, and (2) guarded — the identical LLM proposal validated by a deterministic netops verifier with up to one automated repair if a preregistered high/medium-severity violation was detected. Primary outcome: verifier pass (no preregistered high/medium-severity violations). Results (complete pairs = 500): baseline passed 499/500 (0.998), guarded passed 500/500 (1.000); contingency counts n11 = 499, n10 = 1, n01 = 0, n00 = 0. Absolute paired success-rate difference (guarded − baseline) = 0.002; paired-bootstrap 95% percentile CI = [0.0, 0.006] (B = 10,000, seed = 1729). Under the preregistered exact-binomial-on-discordant-pairs convention the two-sided McNemar p = 1.00. Interpretation: for this verifier-scoped synthetic corpus and the model+validator pairing, the LLM produced near-ceiling proposals; a modest verifier+repair budget produced a small measurable pass-rate improvement while concretely correcting one baseline failure. All preregistration, prompts, model outputs, validator traces, provider-call logs, execution logs, and analysis artifacts are archived in the study evidence bundle.

sections.introduction: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly proposed and deployed for NetOps tasks—translating operator intent into device configuration, planning multi-step changes, and performing limited automated repairs. Operational safety in these agentic-NETOPS pipelines depends not only on model capability but on surrounding engineering: deterministic validators, sandbox replay, canarying, and rollback mechanisms. The generate→verify→repair (G→V→R) architectural pattern places a deterministic verifier between generation and enactment and optionally applies automated repairs for detected violations. Despite conceptual consensus that guardrails are valuable, practitioners lack controlled measurements that isolate the verifier’s marginal contribution when holding the LLM proposal fixed. We conducted a preregistered paired experiment to answer a focused, operational question: given identical initial LLM proposals (shared_initial_candidate semantics), how much does integrating a deterministic verifier and at most one automated repair iteration reduce verifier-detected safety violations compared to the same LLM alone?
sections.related_work: Deterministic network-configuration verifiers (e.g., header-space and route-model analyzers) have a long history of detecting reachability and update-safety violations prior to deployment [https://doi.org/10.1145/3098822.3098834]. Recent NetOps and AIOps work documents LLM-based intent translation and automated configuration synthesis while emphasizing the need for operational guardrails and validation in production-like workflows [https://doi.org/10.1145/3718958.3750537; http://arxiv.org/abs/2309.05557]. Generate–validate–repair (or generate–critic) patterns are advocated across structured-generation domains to reduce unsafe outputs; related system descriptions and surveys argue that the combination of LLMs with deterministic analyzers is a promising path for operationalization [http://arxiv.org/abs/2605.12729; https://openalex.org/W7161165783]. Separate literature catalogs LLM failure modes (hallucination, overconfidence, tool-integration errors) and prescribes verification or human oversight as mitigations [https://doi.org/10.2139/ssrn.6484501]. What is less common are preregistered controlled ablations that keep the model output identical across arms and quantify the isolated verifier+repair effect on deterministic verifier-scoped properties; this study addresses that gap using an artifact-backed confirmatory design.
sections.methodology:
Preregistration and design. The study was preregistered prior to execution (study_id cand_7f4b9a2d_hosted_gvr_v1_2026). We preregistered inclusion/exclusion rules, sampling, estimands, seeds, analysis procedures, and the confirmatory test. The primary estimand is the paired_success_rate_difference_guarded_minus_baseline, where per-task success is defined as the verifier reporting zero preregistered high- or medium-severity violations over the verifier-modeled property set.

Task corpus and stratification. A deterministic synthetic generator produced 500 confirmatory intent→configuration tasks with fixed seeds and stratified across three clusters: VLAN-change (167), ACL-change (167), and static-route-change (166). Generator constraints limited task payloads to the verifier-covered fields {admin, mtu, vlan} to ensure construct validity for the chosen deterministic validator.

Generation semantics and isolation of verifier effect. To measure the marginal contribution of verification and a limited repair budget we used shared_initial_candidate semantics: each task had a single LLM-generated proposal that served as both the baseline output and the guarded arm’s input. The guarded arm invoked an automated single-repair attempt only when the verifier flagged a preregistered high- or medium-severity violation on that shared candidate. This prevents conflation with verifier-guided regeneration and isolates the effect of deterministic verification plus at most one repair applied to the same proposal.

Model and verifier. The requested LLM was gpt-5-mini (hosted adapter) with single-attempt generation and a 2,000-token output limit. The verifier was a purpose-built deterministic netops validator mapping concrete violation codes to preassigned severity levels; the guarded condition applied at most one automated repair iteration per preregistered contract.

Confirmatory inference and resampling. The preregistered primary test is an exact McNemar two-sided test implemented as an exact binomial on the discordant-pair count (n = n10 + n01) with the two-sided p-value convention described in the preregistration. Complementary uncertainty quantification used a paired-bootstrap percentile 95% confidence interval for the absolute paired difference with B = 10,000 resamples and seed = 1729 while preserving pairing. The analysis executor and scripts were frozen prior to data collection and archived.
sections.results:
Execution accounting. Under shared_initial_candidate semantics the run produced 500 complete paired tasks. Model-call accounting recorded 501 hosted model calls: 500 shared-initial generations and exactly 1 repair-stage call (model_calls_used = 501; observed repair-stage calls = 1).

Primary outcomes. Aggregate per-condition verifier pass counts: baseline passed 499/500 (0.998), guarded passed 500/500 (1.000). Paired contingency counts: n11 = 499 (both pass), n10 = 1 (guarded pass only), n01 = 0 (baseline pass only), n00 = 0 (both fail). Absolute paired success-rate difference (guarded − baseline) = 0.0020000000000000018.

Inferential results. Under the preregistered exact-binomial-on-discordant-pairs convention the two-sided McNemar p-value for the observed discordant counts (n = 1, n10 = 1) is p = 1.00. The paired-bootstrap percentile 95% CI for the absolute difference is [0.0, 0.006] (B = 10,000, seed = 1729). These analyses follow the preregistered estimand and implementation choices archived with the study artifacts.

Repair provenance. The single repair-stage call produced the sole discordant outcome: one task where the baseline failed and the guarded arm passed. Per-task validator diagnostics and the repair trace for that episode are archived; run-level reconciliation confirms exactly one corrected episode in the confirmatory set. Secondary analyses by violation class were uninformative because the observed baseline violation prevalence (1/500) was far lower than the preregistered anticipated rate (~30%), producing a ceiling effect and low power to detect small absolute improvements.
sections.discussion:
Conditional interpretation and operational meaning. The measurement is conditional on several constrained design choices: a single requested LLM (gpt-5-mini requested), shared_initial_candidate semantics, a deterministic verifier modeling a limited feature set (allowed_fields = {admin, mtu, vlan}), and at most one automated repair iteration. Within this constrained regime the LLM produced near-ceiling correct proposals on the verifier-scoped properties; consequently the marginal verifier+repair effect on the composite pass/fail metric is numerically small (0.002) yet operationally meaningful because the verifier+repair corrected at least one concrete baseline failure. The paired-bootstrap CI [0.0, 0.006] and the exact-binomial McNemar p = 1.00 reflect wide relative uncertainty driven by the ceiling effect and the small number of discordant pairs.

Design trade-offs and semantics. The shared_initial_candidate semantics intentionally address deployment scenarios where preserving the original model proposal (for audit or human review) and minimizing extra model calls matter. Alternative semantics—verifier-guided regeneration, larger automated-repair budgets, or iterative model–verifier loops—would change model-call accounting and likely alter final-pass probabilities; those operational choices should be evaluated under separate preregistrations that match their cost and safety trade-offs.

Threats to validity and generalization. Construct validity is limited by verifier coverage: success (no high/medium-severity violations) is defined relative to the verifier’s modeled properties and severity mapping. If operator-critical constraints lie outside those modeled features (vendor-specific CLI quirks, dynamic protocol state), the measured pass-rate difference underestimates the potential operational value of broader verifier coverage. External validity is limited by single-model testing (requested gpt-5-mini), a synthetic deterministic task corpus, and constrained feature scope; we do not claim cross-model, cross-vendor, or unconstrained-production generality. The large discrepancy between the preregistered expected baseline error prevalence (~30%) and observed prevalence (1/500) produced a ceiling effect that undermined the preregistered power assumptions and left many secondary analyses uninformative.

Practical implications. First, measure baseline proposal error prevalence for verifier-scoped properties on representative operational data before choosing repair budgets: extremely low baseline error rates limit marginal return on modest verifier+repair investments. Second, align verifier coverage with operator-critical properties; expanding verifier-modeled fields can increase observable verifier benefit. Third, select generation semantics that match deployment priorities: shared_initial_candidate semantics reduce model-call cost and preserve the original proposal, while verifier-guided regeneration or iterative repair increases model-call cost but can raise final-pass probability.

Evidence-grounded recommendations. Operators planning LLM-enabled NetOps should (a) benchmark baseline verifier-scoped error rates on representative workloads, (b) choose verifier coverage to target operationally important classes of violations, and (c) memoize the chosen generate/repair semantics (shared-initial vs regenerate) into deployment SLAs so that cost, auditability, and human-review workflows are consistent with safety goals.
sections.conclusion: We executed a preregistered paired experiment (N = 500) that isolated the verifier+single-repair effect under shared_initial_candidate semantics. The LLM produced near-ceiling verifier-scoped proposals (baseline 499/500; guarded 500/500), yielding an absolute improvement of 0.002 with a paired-bootstrap 95% CI of [0.0, 0.006] and an archived exact McNemar two-sided p = 1.00 under the preregistered exact-binomial convention. The results illustrate a ceiling-effect regime: when baseline proposal quality is already very high for the verifier-modeled properties and the verifier’s scope is limited, a modest verifier+repair budget can produce only small measurable gains on a composite pass/fail metric while still being capable of correcting rare concrete failures. Practitioners should estimate baseline error prevalence on representative workloads, align verifier coverage with critical operator constraints, and select generation/repair semantics that match deployment cost and auditability priorities. All preregistration, prompts, model outputs, validator traces, provider-call logs, execution logs, and analysis artifacts are archived in the study evidence bundle for deterministic re-inspection of the claims above.

limitations: Synthetic deterministic task corpus limited to the verifier-modeled features; task payloads were constrained to allowed_fields = {admin, mtu, vlan}. Results do not generalize to unconstrained production intents, wider cross-vendor CLI heterogeneity, or dynamic protocol states outside the verifier scope.
Single requested model family (gpt-5-mini requested) and a single deterministic validator (deterministic_netops_validator_v5) — we do not claim multi-model or cross-validator generality.
Maximum one automated repair iteration was permitted by the preregistration; different repair budgets or iterative regeneration strategies could change measured verifier impact.

Very high baseline pass rate (499/500) induced a ceiling effect that limits power to detect small absolute improvements on the pass-rate metric; the archived exact McNemar two-sided p = 1.00 reflects the preregistered exact-binomial-on-discordant-pairs convention and the small discordant count.

The single discordant episode (the sole task where baseline failed and guarded succeeded) and its validator diagnostics and repair-stage trace are archived in the study evidence bundle. The run-level manifest and per-task scoring traces confirm exactly one such corrected episode in the confirmatory set.
